prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reach fractional frequency uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part for the optical lattice clock, credited to Katori and Ye. After the full exchange I hold it more firmly, and for scientific reasons rather than because six of eight members now agree. The physics is a clean idea (the magic-wavelength condition cancels the light shift of the trapping field) followed by a quantitative programme in which blackbody, collisional and lattice shifts were each measured and cross-checked. The result has been reproduced and surpassed in independent laboratories, and clock-to-clock comparisons agree near 1e-18. That is the reproducibility test I apply to any result. The attribution is the least contested on the shortlist and all proposers named the same pair. The chair's question on overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes has a workable answer: those prizes honoured spectroscopy with combs and control of single trapped quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock solved the separate problem of interrogating very many neutral atoms without perturbing the clock transition. The citation should name that contribution and stay silent on applications that have not yet been realised, which meets Olsson's wish to keep prospective uses out of the wording.
statement.case_against: The overlap with earlier metrology prizes does not disappear because the citation is careful. Some members will read the lattice clock as an extremely successful refinement and not a new phenomenon, and I cannot rule that reading out; it is a judgment about kinds of discovery and not a measurable fact. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so the societal payoff is still prospective, and the dark-matter and constants searches have so far given bounds. Early contributors, in particular Lemonde and Takamoto, sit outside the two names and I cannot settle their priority myself, so I would want the expert reports to confirm that no claim is strong enough to change the credit. Finally, topological insulators (B058) remain, to me, the deeper physics of a new class of matter, and I keep it as my first alternative. Its attribution problem (Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang on HgTe, and the three-dimensional work) is not solved by any three-name split I have seen in this discussion.

responses.point: Kroll argues that earlier prizes did not cover trapping many neutral atoms without perturbing the clock transition, and asks how I would settle the B058 credit within three names.
responses.response: His distinction between the earlier prizes and the lattice clock is the argument I would use in the citation, and it moves me toward treating the overlap worry as a wording problem and not a bar. On B058 I have no clean answer to his question: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leave out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp tested, and I cannot defend a three-name set that drops them. That is why B058 is an alternative and not my preferred choice. I would still ask him, as the committee's atomic-physics experimentalist, to confirm that his own year in Hall's laboratory does not need to be handled as a recusal on B030.

responses.point: Olsson wants applications left out of the citation, regards the clock's value as mainly metrological and prospective, and notes that priority outside the credited names is not entirely closed.
responses.response: I agree on the citation: it should name the lattice clock and its realization and the demonstrated accuracy, and not the redefinition of the second or the constants and dark-matter searches. On priority, I read her concern the same way I read my own: until expert reviewers speak, I treat Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others as a risk to the two-name credit and not a settled non-issue. Her fellowship in Tokyo, with no personal tie to Katori, seems to me a disclosure for the record and not grounds for recusal, but the chair should decide that openly.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube (B020) to B030 because maturity, attribution and breadth of support line up, while stating that he cannot settle fine points of atomic-physics priority.
responses.response: I respect that he separated the count from the science, and I share his deference: I am a materials theorist and I do not claim authority on atomic-physics priority either. His question about a second part is the important one for my configuration. I looked for a pairing with B020 or B058 inside the three-person limit and could not find a fair one, because adding either would require splitting names that already have unresolved credit. Adding a second part for the sake of balance would weaken the clean attribution that makes B030 strong, so I stay with a single part. If IceCube's credit is confirmed by experts against AMANDA and Baikal, I would revisit it in a future cycle and not combine it now.

responses.point: Mehlig remains the only member preferring KPZ (B049) and presents it as a minority view while keeping B030 and B058 as alternatives.
responses.response: I find his case for KPZ scientifically attractive: a simple mechanism, exact one-dimensional results and the Tracy-Widom confirmation in liquid-crystal turbulence. My difficulty is still attribution, because Parisi, a 1986 co-author and 2021 laureate, is outside Kardar and Zhang, and Spohn's later exact-solution work is a separate achievement. I would not want to dismiss the candidacy, but I do not think it can be given a fair three-person form this year, and his own retention of B030 and B058 as alternatives suggests we are not far apart.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B030 and discloses a clear connection to circuit QED (B029) and a lesser one to B044, proposing to discount his own B029 ranking.
responses.response: I support his proposal to discount his B029 ranking, and I note that his move to B030 rests on the same chain of reasoning as mine: a clean idea followed by understood systematics. I agree with his remark that the 2016 topology prize makes B058 closer to a sequel, and it is one reason I keep B058 as an alternative rather than my first choice.

uncertainties: Whether expert reports on priority will find that Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow or others have a claim strong enough to alter the two-name credit.
Whether the committee accepts a precision-measurement invention as a discovery or invention in the statutory sense, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
How the citation should describe the respective roles of Katori (proposal and first demonstration) and Ye (record accuracy and many-body regime) without turning it into a ranking.
Whether the committee prefers a new state of matter (B058, B057) over a precision instrument this year, which I cannot settle by measurement.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second will change the maturity case before the final ballot.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. I am at Uppsala, and I have no known tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist; my connections (Johansson, Los Alamos, Bergman, Bergqvist, Hellsvik, Delin) are not linked to any shortlisted candidate. I chaired the committee for the 2025 prize. I have read the disclosures of Olsson, Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson and Pearce and regard them as matters for the chair's judgment; none of them alters my own position.
